# Estimating density as a latent variable from overdispersed acoustic detection counts
## Packages
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dclone) 
library(rjags) 
```

## Framework

Imagine we will sample birds ($s$) during the morning (05:00-9:50) of every possible day ($t$) at their breeding territory, and the birds defend that territory across the breeding season of that year ($t = 1 \mapsto T$). We can use point-counts and Passive Acoustic Monitoring in the same sites $m$. These two observation processes should link with the ecological process (latent) of the abundance of individuals available to be detected and providing cues of their presence, which will be assumed to be stationary during the sampling period (every morning of day $t$ during the breeding season). Evidently, some mornings and sampling events $t_i$ will have stochastic variation, reflecting a noise in the process that could be also accounted for. From empirical data, we have seeing that point counts could be underdispersed (0 < Variance-to-Mean Ratio < 1; Binomial) to uniformly dispersed (Variance-to-Mean Ration = 1; Poisson), while acoustic detections are overdispersed (Variance-to-Mean Ration >> 1; Negative Binomial).

```{r}
# Gompertz functions
gompertz <- function(t, K = 1, a = 5, b = 0.5) {
  K * exp(-a * exp(-b * t))
}

gompertz_decay <- function(t, K = 1, a = 5, b = 0.5) {
  K - gompertz(t, K, a, b)
}

# Time
t1 <- seq(0, 20, length.out = 200)
t2 <- seq(20, 40, length.out = 200)

# Deterministic mean curve
mu_vec <- c(
  gompertz(t1, K = 0.5, a = 5, b = 0.4),
  gompertz_decay(t2 - 20, K = 0.5, a = 5, b = 0.4)
)

# Add stochasticity (process noise)
set.seed(123)
sigma_proc <- 0.03
latent_stochastic <- mu_vec + rnorm(length(mu_vec), 0, sigma_proc)

# Sampling window
stationary_start <- 9
stationary_end   <- 21

# Sampling indices
sample_idx <- sample(125:175, size = 17)

acoustic_vec <- rep(NA, length(mu_vec))
counts_vec   <- rep(NA, length(mu_vec))

acoustic_vec[sample_idx] <- rnorm(17, mean = 0.65, sd = 0.5)
counts_vec[sample_idx]   <- rnorm(17, mean = 0.25, sd = 0.1)

df <- tibble(
  time     = c(t1, t2),
  mu       = mu_vec,
  latent   = latent_stochastic,
  acoustic = acoustic_vec,
  counts   = counts_vec
)

# Plot
ggplot(df, aes(time)) +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = stationary_start-0.5, xmax = stationary_end+0.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#00000010",
           color = "#00000020") +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = 12.5, xmax = 17.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#ADD8E640",
           color = "#ADD8E660") +
  geom_line(aes(y = latent,
                color = "Latent",
                fill = "Latent",
                shape = "Latent"),
            size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mu,
                color = "Mean",
                fill = "Mean",
                shape = "Mean"),
            linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = acoustic,
                 color = "Acoustic",
                 fill = "Acoustic",
                 shape = "Acoustic"),
             size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = counts,
                 color = "Counts",
                 fill = "Counts",
                 shape = "Counts"),
             size = 2) +
   annotate("text", x = c(10.5,19.5), y = 0.71, label = "Breeding", color = "#00000060") +
   annotate("text", x = 15, y = 0.01, label = "Sampling", color = "#72bcd4") +
   annotate("text", x = c(3,27), y = 0.41, label = "Non-breeding", color = "#00000060") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean" = "black",
                                "Latent" = "gray50",
                                "Acoustic" = "#1B9E77",
                                "Counts" = "#D95F02")) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean" = "black",
                                "Latent" = "gray50",
                                "Acoustic" = "#1B9E7760",
                                "Counts" = "#D95F0260")) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean" = NA,
                                "Latent" = NA,
                                "Acoustic" = 24,
                                "Counts" = 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,30)) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Abundance") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.85,0.8),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank())
ggsave(filename = "figs/Framework.jpg", 
       width = 1800, height = 900, units = "px", dpi = 300)
```

![Framework for estimating latent density from two observation process using stochastic GSS](figs/Framework.jpg)

Here we want to estimate the latent abundance (black line of the figure) from overdispersed acoustic detection counts from passive acoustic monitoring (orange upward triangles). We can compare the estimated latent abundance from underdispersed counts from point counts (purple downward triangles). This figure is fake data, with the unique purpose of present our framework and ecological rationale.

## Ecological process

Let's assume that we have sites of sampling $m = 1,2,~...~,~M$ and species $s = 1,2,~...~,S$ in an area. Our latent state $X_{m,s} = \log{(N_{m,s})}$ is the site-level log-abundance state for species $s$ at the site $m$. This could be a temporal dynamic follows a stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, OU, diffusion process for stochastic Gompertz function on the log-scale across time $t$, which represent days within the breeding season. Sampling can occur at subtemporal units $t_i$, representing 10-min duration each morning (see [Dennis & Ponciano 2014](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/13-1486.1) and [Acevedo-Charry et al. 2025](https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.70108) for examples of this models for population dynamics):

$$
X_{t+1, m, s} = a_s + c_s * X_{t, m, s} + \epsilon_{t};\\ 
~ \epsilon_t \sim \text{Normal}(0,\sigma_s^2)
$$

where $a_s$ control the drift (the initial condition at $t=1$, and then it is equivalent to the maximum growth rate in a population model), $c_s$ controls the mean-reverting dynamic (such as the strength of density dependence, $c_s = 1 + b_s$ in a population model), and $\epsilon_{t}$ captures stochasticity in the process, distributed as a (log) normal random variable with some noise of the process as variance $\sigma_s^2$. Under stationarity and independence across sites, we can estimate the mean of the log-abundance as a function of the control drift and mean-reverting dynamic:

$$
\text{E}[X_{\infty, m, s}] = \mu_s= \frac{a_s}{1-c_s}
$$
This stationary value is represented as the dashed gray line tracking the latent dynamic (black line) in the framework figure during the sampling period.

We can also estimate the variance of this value:

$$
\text{Var}[X_{\infty, m, s}] = \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2}
$$

We can simulate a community by sampling $X_{t,m,s}$ i.i.d. (independent and identical distributed) across $m$ from this stationary distribution. Dealing with the Janzen's inequality, we can add half of the variance to the $\hat{\mu_s}$. The expected abundance per site $m$ of each species $s$ becomes:

$$
\text{E}[\lambda_{m,s}] = \exp \left( \mu_s + 0.5 \times \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2} \right)
$$

But to simulate observed data, we can initiate the time-series with the realized latent state at $t = 1$:
$$
X_{1,m,s} \sim \text{Normal} \left(\mu_s, \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2} \right) \\

\lambda_{1,m,s} = \exp(X_{1,m,s})
$$

and the temporal trajectory within a site across the sampling period of ~30 days $t = 1, ..., T = 30$ (with 30 blocks of 10-minutes each morning, 05:00 to 09:50, for 30 days, scales to  $t_i = 1, ..., T_i(m) = 900$) looks like: 

$$
X_{t, m, s} = a_s + c_sX_{t-1,m,s} + \epsilon_{t,s}, \\
\epsilon_{t,s} \sim \text{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_{t,s})
$$
and each time has its own realized latent state:
$$
\lambda_{t,m,s} = \exp(X_{t,m,s})
$$

This latent state should be similar between the two observation processes in case of a 1:1 relationship of the acoustic detection rate and the expected counts ( $\lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Counts}} \approx \lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} \times 1$). But if the species is acoustically active, it is clear to expect that there is a scaling parameter $\alpha_s$ between them ($\lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} = \exp(X_{t,m,s}) \times \alpha_s \approx \lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Counts}}$) 

## Observation processes

In our thought experiment, we can conduct point counts in an approximated area of 0.78 ha, equivalent from a 50m fixed radius (see [Lopez et al. 2017](https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12856)). The point-count observed counts are 
$$
N^{\text{Count temp}}_{t,m,s} = \max(1,\lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Counts}}); \\

Y_{t_i,m,s}^{\text{Counts}} \sim \text{Binomial}(N^{\text{Count temp}}_{t,m,s}, \tau_{s})\\
\text{or}\\
Y_{t_i,m,s}^{\text{Counts}} \sim \text{Poisson}(\tau_{s} \times \lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Counts}})\\
$$ 
\noindent where $\tau_{s}$ ranges between 0 and 1, and is a species-specific detection probability. It could be reasonable to assume additional differences across site ($\tau_{m,s}$), but that would over complicates the model for now. Other models (Royle-Nichols, TTD, N-mixture, hierarchical distance, see [Fiss et al. 2017](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ecs2.4954)) also assume equal detection probability across individuals and visits.

On the other hand, the acoustic detection data are 
$$
\lambda_{m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} = \exp(X_{t,m,s}) \times \alpha_s; \\
Y_{t_i,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} \sim \text{Negative Binomial}(\lambda_{m,s}^{\text{Acoust}},\pi_s)
$$
\noindent where $\alpha_s$ represents a scaling factor between acoustic counts and abundance (close to the acoustic detection rate of the species in a region?), $\pi_s$ is the "size" overdispersion parameter and $\lambda_{m,s}^{\text{Acoust}}$ represents the expected number of counts (mean ecological parametrization). Note that in conventional notation (e.g., Bolker's Book), the expected number of counts for the Negative Binomial distribution is $\mu$, while the overdispersion parameter "size" is $k$; so the probability of success in each trial is $p^{\text{NegBinom}} = \frac{k}{(k+\mu)}$. We modified this notation to be consistent with the notation for the Poisson distribution (the expected counts are $\lambda^{\text{Poisson}} \approx \mu^{\text{NegBin}}$) and avoid confusion with the notation of the Gompertz state-space model and data cloning ($\mu$ is the log-abundance stationary mean; $k^{\text{NegBin}} \approx \pi^{\text{Here}} \neq k^{\text{Data Cloning}}~\text{clones}$).

Thus, during the breeding season (e.g., middle May to middle June), we have the possibility to sample each site 30 times between 05:00 and 09:50 for several mornings, including various visits per site (higher possibilities for passive acoustic monitoring than point counts!). These 10-min duration sampling events generate the point counts (Binomial or Poisson) and acoustic detection count (Negative Binomial) data in a simultaneous design. To accelerate the simulation, let's select a single point count per day in 30 days, intensely sampled (25-30 days); we will revisit this in a sensitivity analysis.

## Simulating some data

Define sites $M$ and species $S$. For now, we can consider only 2 species, just to check the visual differences of the latent variable among them.
```{r}
set.seed(123)
M <- 10
S <- 2
T_max <- 30

visits <- sample(29:30, M, replace = TRUE) 
T_m <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))
  
for(s in 1:S){
  for(m in 1:M){
    sample_idx <- sort(sample(1:T_max, size = visits[m], replace = FALSE))
    sample_vec <- rep(NA, T_max)
    sample_vec[sample_idx] <- 1
    T_m[,m,s] <- sample_vec
  }
}

head(T_m)
```

This object represent sampling visits (with 1) to 10 sites for two species.

### Species-level parameters

To get stable equilibrium density dynamics (when $t \rightarrow \infty$, the log abundance $x_t \rightarrow \mu$), the mean-reversing parameter should be $|c_s|<1$. When $0<c<1$, the log-abundance approaches to equilibrium directly. In contrast, when $-1<c<0$ the dynamic follows a damped oscillatory behavior (see [Ponciano et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tpb.2018.04.002)). A mean-reversing parameter $c = 1$ identify exponential dynamics. Based on our assumption that individuals already arrived to their territories and are defending them, we could also assume that the mean-reversing is not leading to damped oscillatory behavior nor exponential dynamics, so ranging $0.1 < c < 0.9$. We can rely on the infinitesimal relationship $\theta = -\log(c)$ of the OUSS Gaussian diffusion process [(Dennis & Ponciano 2014)](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/13-1486.1).   

We know that the stationary mean log-abundance $\mu_s = \frac{a_s}{1-c_s}$. Thus, if we can "force" a mean log-abundance reasonable (such as between $\log(0.5)$ and $\log(10)$; see Fig 3 in [Fiss et al. 2017](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ecs2.4954)). Let's use $\mu \sim \text{Normal}(\log(3.14),0.3)$ to initiate the mean stationary log-abundance (similar to the simulation in [Chandler et al. 2011](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/10-2433.1)).

With these two parameters, we can compute $a_s = \mu \times c_s$.

For the environmental stochasticity noise, we can use the ranges reported in [Dennis et al. (2006)](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/0012-9615%282006%2976%5B323%3AEDDPNA%5D2.0.CO%3B2) and/or [Dennis et al. (2017)](http://www.math.ualberta.ca/~slele/publications/Lele%20Dennis%20Lutscher%20data%20cloning%20Ecology%20Letters%2020071.pdf), $\sigma_s^2$ between $0.001$ and $0.3$. We can use $\log(\sigma^2) \sim \text{Normal}(\log(0.05),0.3)$.

With these parameters, we can draw process $X_{t,m,s}$

```{r}
set.seed(123)
# for the OU latent variable, we can rely on 
lmu <- rnorm(S, log(5), 1)
ltheta <- rnorm(S, log(0.3), 0.2)
lsigsq <- rnorm(S, log(0.05), 0.3)

mu_s <- lmu             # mean stationary log-abundance
theta_s <- exp(ltheta)  # spead of equilibrium
sigsq_s <- exp(lsigsq)  # noise of environmental stochasticity

K_s <- exp(mu_s)        # mean stationary abundance
c_s <- exp(-theta_s)    # mean-reversion parameter
a_s <- mu_s * (1 - c_s) # control the drift 

var_statio_s <- sigsq_s / (1 - exp(-2 * theta_s))

X <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S)) 

for(s in 1:S){ 
  for(m in 1:M){
    # first visit, drawn from the stationary distribution
    X[1,m,s] <- rnorm(1, mean = mu_s[s], sd = sqrt(var_statio_s[s]))
    
    # OU recursion process moving throughout time
    for(t in 2:T_max){
      X[t,m,s] <- rnorm(1, mean = (a_s[s] + c_s[s]*X[t-1,m,s]), sd = sqrt(sigsq_s))
    }
  }
}
head(X)
```

This is the latent log-abundance of two species in each site across the 30 days.

Expected density per species per site at each time of visit, in original scale.
```{r}
lambda <- exp(X)
cool.palette <- as.vector(MetBrewer::met.brewer("Homer2",10))

jpeg("figs/Simulate_2s_10m_30t.jpeg", 
    width = 800, height = 650, units = "px", res = 150)
par(mfrow = c(1,2),oma=c(5,5,4,1), mar=c(2,2,2,1))

for(s in 1:S){
  plot(1:T_max, lambda[,1,s], 
     pch=16, type="b",  bty="l",
     xlab="", ylab="", main = paste0("Species ", s),
     ylim=c(0,10), col=alpha(cool.palette[1], 0.5), cex.lab=1.15)
  for(m in 2:M){ # only 10 of the 100 sites
    points(1:T_max, lambda[,m,s],
           pch = 16, type = "b", col = alpha(cool.palette[m], 0.5))
  }
}
mtext(text = "Latent expected abundance (10 sites)", side=2, outer=TRUE, cex=1.25,line=1)
mtext(text = "Time (30 days)", side=1, outer=TRUE, cex=1.25,line=1)
dev.off() 
```
![Simulated expected latent abundance of four species in 30 sites](figs/Simulate_2s_10m_30t.jpeg)

Even though the latent expected abundance is around 5, these two species show stochastic expected counts and heterogeneity among sites (colors).

### Observation process by point counts

Recall:
$$
N^{\text{Count temp}}_{t,m,s} = \max(1,\lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Counts}}); \\

Y_{t_i,m,s}^{\text{Counts}} \sim \text{Binomial}(N^{\text{Count temp}}_{t,m,s}, \tau_{s})\\
\text{or}\\
Y_{t_i,m,s}^{\text{Counts}} \sim \text{Poisson}(\tau_{s} \times \lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Counts}})\\
$$ 

We need the detection probability parameter $\tau_{s}$. Although detection probabilities for North-American birds distributes with right-skew shape, we can use a simple normal distribution with mean 0.3 and sd = 0.05 across species (this is similar to the simulated by [Chandler et al. 2011](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/10-2433.1)).

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
# Species-level mean detectability 
tau_s <- rnorm(S, 0.3, 0.05)

Y_counts <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))

for(s in 1:S){
  for(m in 1:M){
    for(t in 1:T_max){ 
      if(!is.na(T_m[t,m,s])){# only visited sites
        # point counts Binomial detection
        N_bin <- max(1,round(lambda[t,m,s]))
        Y_counts[t,m,s] <- rbinom(1,N_bin ,tau_s[s])
      }
    }
  }
}

head(Y_counts)
```
This shows a simulated observation matrix of four species sampled across 15 sites, where NA indicates that the site was not sampled at that period of time for that species.

### Observation process by acoustic detections counts

Recall:
$$
\lambda_{m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} = \exp(X_{t,m,s}) \times \alpha_s; \\
Y_{t_i,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} \sim \text{Negative Binomial}(\lambda_{m,s}^{\text{Acoust}},\pi_s)
$$

We can estimate the acoustic detection rate (acoustic detection counts per minute), for example for species 1 could be 3.198 (range from 2.310 to 3.770), whereas for species 2 could be 1.490 (range from 1.300 to 1.670). We can convert these ranges in the SD of an assumed normal distribution by dividing the range of values by 4 (SD_1 = 0.365; SD_2 = 0.0925).  

We also need the overdispersion parameter $\pi_s$. The variance for a Negative Binomial is $\text{Var}(Y) = \lambda+\frac{\lambda^2}{\pi_s}$, being $\lambda$ the expected value (mean $\text{E}(Y) = \lambda = n\frac{(1-p)}{p}$, where $p$ is the probability per trial and $n$ the number of success awaited; see "ecological" parameterization in Bolker's book). The Variance-to-Mean Ratio is $\text{VMR} = \frac{\text{Var}(Y)}{\text{E}(Y)} = \frac{\lambda + \frac{\lambda^2}{\pi_s}}{\lambda} = 1+\frac{\lambda}{\pi_s}$. Thus, the "size" overdispersion parameter can be estimated as $\pi_s = \frac{\lambda}{\text{VMR}-1}$.

To select this overdispersion parameter, we can use the simulated $5$ and an empirical $\text{VMR} = [5.17-50.86]$, thus $\pi_{lower} = \frac{5}{5.17-1} = 1.19904$ to $\pi_{upper} = \frac{5}{50.86-1} = 0.10028$. The lower $\pi$, the higher overdispersion, while if $\pi \rightarrow \infty$, the distribution tend to a Poisson ($\text{VMR} \rightarrow 1$).

```{r}
set.seed(1234)

alpha_s <- vector()
alpha_s[1] <- rnorm(1, 3.198, 0.365) 
alpha_s[2] <- rnorm(1, 1.490, 0.0925) 

pi_s <- rnorm(S, 0.40, 0.15)

Y_acoust <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))

for(s in 1:S){
  for(m in 1:M){
    for(t in 1:T_max){
      if(!is.na(T_m[t,m,s])){ #only visited
      Y_acoust[t,m,s] <- rnbinom(1, mu = (lambda[t,m,s] * alpha_s[s]), size = pi_s[s])
      }
    }
  }
}
head(Y_acoust)
```

### Check the Variance-to-Mean Ration (VMR) of this simulated dataset

```{r}

ggsave(filename = "figs/Simulating_Latent_Observed.jpg", 
       width = 150, height = 100, units = "mm")

# Remove NA values in the array of counts
df_clean <- df |>
  filter(!is.na(Y_counts))

# Compute VMR per species
vmr_df <- df_clean |>
  group_by(s) |>
  summarise(
    meanCounts  = mean(Y_counts),
    varCounts   = var(Y_counts),
    VMR_counts  = varCounts / meanCounts,

    meanAcoust  = mean(Y_acoust),
    varAcoust   = var(Y_acoust),
    VMR_acoust  = varAcoust / meanAcoust
  )

as.data.frame(vmr_df)
```

## Fit a stochastic GSS model to recover simulated the parameters

Let's prove if we can recover the parameters for one species ($s=1$). We need a model that represent our stochastic GSS (OU) in a datacloning framework. First, select the species.

```{r}
sp1 <- 1

Yc_s <- Y_counts[ , , sp1]
Ya_s <- Y_acoust[ , , sp1]
# Confirming NA-masking for not visited sites at some times
Yc_s[is.na(T_m[,,sp1])] <- NA
Ya_s[is.na(T_m[,,sp1])] <- NA

```

### Fit model for counts (our business as usual to compare)

Let's fit first a "Counts" model

```{r Stochastic GSS model for data cloning fitting of point counts}
CountOU.dc <- function() {

  # Priors (no cloning)
  lmu ~ dnorm(log(5), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  ltheta ~ dnorm(log(0.3), 1/(0.2^2)) # in precision terms
  lsigsq ~ dnorm(log(0.05), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
#  ltau ~ dnorm(log(0.3/(1-0.3)), 1/(0.5^2)) # logit-normal 
  
#  tau <- 1/(1+exp(-ltau))  # detection probability
  tau <- 0.3 #fixing tau close to true value to evaluate convergence and informability
  mu <- lmu
  theta <- exp(ltheta)
  sigsq <- exp(lsigsq)
  
  c <- exp(-theta)
  a <- mu * (1-c)
  Vinf <- sigsq/(1-exp(-2 * theta))
  
  # Likelihood (data cloning)
  for (k in 1:K) {               # K = clones
    for (m in 1:M) {             # M = sites
      
      # Stationary distribution for t=1
      X1[1,m,k] ~ dnorm(mu, 1 / Vinf) # JAGS works with precision

      # State process over time
      for (t in 2:qp1) {
        X1[t,m,k] ~ dnorm((a + c * X1[t-1,m,k]), 1 / sigsq) # JAGS works with precision
      }

      # Observation processes
      for (t in 1:qp1) {
        # latent abundance with a Poisson detection, 
          # because Binomial detection was causing Node problems in JAGS
        Y_counts[t,m,k] ~ dpois(exp(X1[t,m,k]) * tau)
     }
    }
  }
}

```

And we can bundle the data and fit the model with data cloning. 
```{r, eval=FALSE}
# initialize some values
inits.c <- list(
  list(lmu=1.1,  ltheta=-1.3, lsigsq=-3.1),
  list(lmu=1.5,  ltheta=-1.1, lsigsq=-2.8),
  list(lmu=1.9,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6)
  )

datalist.dc <- list( 
  K = 1, # clones start at 1 
  M = M, # number of sites 
  qp1 = T_max, # number of time steps 
  Y_counts = dcdim(array(Yc_s, dim = c(T_max,M,1))) #, # [t,m] → [t,m,k]
  )

start_time <- Sys.time()
dcrun.GSS.c <- dc.fit(data = datalist.dc,
                    params = c("c", "a", "sigsq"), 
                   inits = inits.c,
                    model = CountOU.dc, 
                    n.clones = c(1,2,4,8),
                    multiply = "K",
                    unchanged = c("M","qp1"),
                    n.chains = 3,
                    n.adapt = 2000,
                    n.update = 5000,
                    thin = 10,
                    n.iter = 15000)

saveRDS(dcrun.GSS.c, "data/dcfitGSS_Sp1_upto16cl_count_tauFix.rds")

duration_model <- Sys.time()-start_time
print(duration_model)
```

This fit with $T_{max}=30$ and almost complete sampling ($29-30$ days) had a duration of 5 minutes in my laptop (Apple M1 Pro. 16GB).

After several trials, we have found that $\tau_s$ is unidentifiable and generate structural confounding with $\mu$, driving non-convergence of the model estimation. By fixing $\tau_s$, the model stabilizes. When trying a $\tau_s \neq \text{true}$, generates the parameters $\hat{a} = 0.36252 ~ [0.33009-0.3968]$, $\hat{c} = 0.64965 ~ [0.61736-0.6814]$, and $\hat{\sigma^2} = 0.01846 ~ [0.01526-0.0215]$, compared with the true values $a_1=0.353$, $c_1 = 0.664$, $\sigma_1^2 = 0.052$. When using $\tau_s^{\text{fixed}} = 0.3$, the MLEs where $\hat{a} = 0.20632 ~ [0.1498-0.27729]$, $\hat{c} = 0.73723 ~ [0.6527-0.80742]$, and $\hat{\sigma^2} = 0.03428 ~ [0.0215-0.05194]$. Thus, $c$ could be interpreted as robust to $\tau$ choice, suggesting that the temporal dependence is identified from dynamics, not detection probability (i.e., scaling expected counts). This also occur with the process variance $\sigma^2$. 

### Fit model for acoustic detection counts

Let's fit first a "Acoustic" model. In JAGS we have to re-parameterize $\lambda$ and $\pi$ to probability $p^{\text{Negative~binomial}}$.

$$
\lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} = \alpha_s \times \exp(X_{t,m,s}); \\

p^{\text{NegBin}}_{t,m,s} = \frac{\pi_s}{\pi_s+\lambda_{t,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}}}; \\

Y_{t,m,s}^{\text{Acoust}} \sim \text{Negative Binomial}(p^{\text{NegBin}}, \pi_s)\\

$$

```{r Stochastic GSS model for data cloning fitting of point counts}
AcoustOU.dc <- function() {

  # Priors (no cloning)
  lmu ~ dnorm(log(3), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  ltheta ~ dnorm(log(0.3), 1/(0.2^2)) # in precision terms
  lsigsq ~ dnorm(log(0.05), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  pi ~ dnorm(0.17, 1/(0.01^2)) 
  alpha ~ dlnorm(1.0055, 1/(0.53^2)) # scaling between abundance and acoustic counts
  
  mu <- lmu
  theta <- exp(ltheta)
  sigsq <- exp(lsigsq)
  
  c <- exp(-theta)
  a <- mu * (1-c)
  Vinf <- sigsq/(1-exp(-2 * theta))
  
   # Likelihood (data cloning)
  for (k in 1:K) {               # K = clones
    for (m in 1:M) {             # M = sites
      
      # Stationary distribution for t=1
      X1[1,m,k] ~ dnorm(mu, 1 / Vinf) # JAGS works with precision

      # State process over time
      for (t in 2:qp1) {
        X1[t,m,k] ~ dnorm((a + c * X1[t-1,m,k]), 1 / sigsq) # JAGS works with precision
      }

      # Observation processes
      for (t in 1:qp1) {
        # Acoustic Negative Binomial detection
        # we should re-parameterize lambda and pi to p
        # p = pi/(pi+lambda)
        lambda_ac[t,m,k] <- exp(X1[t,m,k]) * alpha
        p_nb[t,m,k] <- pi / (pi + lambda_ac[t,m,k])
        Y_acoust[t,m,k] ~ dnegbin(p_nb[t,m,k], pi)
      }
    }
  }
}

```

And we can bundle the data and fit the model with data cloning.
```{r, eval=FALSE}
# initialize some values

  list(lmu=1.1,  ltheta=-1.3, lsigsq=-3.1, pi = 0.05),
  list(lmu=1.5,  ltheta=-1.1, lsigsq=-2.8, pi = 0.4),
  list(lmu=1.9,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6, pi = 0.75)
  )

datalist.dc.a <- list( 
  K = 1, # clones start at 1 
  M = M, # number of sites 
  qp1 = T_max, # number of time steps 
  Y_acoust = dcdim(array(Ya_s, dim = c(T_max,M,1)))  # [t,m] → [t,m,k]
  )

start_time <- Sys.time()
dcrun.GSS.a <- dc.fit(data = datalist.dc.a,
                    params = c("c", "a", "sigsq", "pi", "alpha"), 
                   inits = inits.a,
                    model = AcoustOU.dc, 
                    n.clones = c(1,2,4,8),
                    multiply = "K",
                    unchanged = c("M","qp1"),
                    n.chains = 3,
                    n.adapt = 2000,
                    n.update = 5000,
                    thin = 10,
                    n.iter = 15000)

saveRDS(dcrun.GSS.a, "data/dcfitGSS_Sp1_upto16cl_acous.rds")

duration_model <- Sys.time()-start_time
print(duration_model)
```

This fit had a duration of 17 minutes in my computer. In the next section, we compare the MLEs.

### Compare latent expected abundance

With the MLEs, we can reconstruct the OU trajectory:

$$
\hat{X}_{m,t} \sim \text{Normal}\left(\frac{\hat{a}}{1-\hat{c}}, \frac{\hat{\sigma^2}}{1-\hat{c}^2}\right); \\

\hat{\lambda}_{t,m} = \exp(\hat{X}_{t,m})
$$

and then compare the latent expected abundance
$$
\lambda_t^{(\text{counts})} ~ \text{vs} ~ \lambda_t^{(\text{acoust})}
$$

```{r}
a_hat_c <- coef(dcrun.GSS.c)[1]
c_hat_c <- coef(dcrun.GSS.c)[2]
sig_hat_c <- coef(dcrun.GSS.c)[3]

mu_hat_c <- a_hat_c / (1 - c_hat_c)
var_hat_c <- sig_hat_c / (1 - c_hat_c^2)

X_hat_c <- matrix(NA, nrow = T_max, ncol = M)

# Initialize from stationary distribution
X_hat_c[1,] <- rnorm(M, mu_hat_c, sqrt(var_hat_c))

# OU/Gompertz dynamics
for (t in 2:T_max){
  X_hat_c[t,] <- rnorm(M, (a_hat_c + c_hat_c * X_hat_c[t-1,]), sqrt(sig_hat_c))
}

lambda_c <- exp(X_hat_c)
```

```{r}
a_hat_a <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a)[1]
c_hat_a <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a)[3]
sig_hat_a <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a)[5]

mu_hat_a <- a_hat_a / (1 - c_hat_a)
var_hat_a <- sig_hat_a / (1 - c_hat_a^2)

X_hat_a <- matrix(NA, nrow = T_max, ncol = M)

# Initialize from stationary distribution
X_hat_a[1,] <- rnorm(M, mu_hat_a, sqrt(var_hat_a))

# OU/Gompertz dynamics
for (t in 2:T_max){
  X_hat_a[t,] <- rnorm(M, (a_hat_a + c_hat_a * X_hat_a[t-1,]), sqrt(sig_hat_a))
}

lambda_a <- exp(X_hat_a)
```

Given the Janzen inequality, we can contrast also the stationary expectations

$$
\text{E}(\lambda_s) = \text{E}[\exp(X_s)] = \exp\left(\mu_s + 0.5 \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2}\right)
$$

```{r}
E_lambda <- exp(mu_s[1] + 0.5 * var_statio_s[1]) # true for the species 1

E_lambda_c <- exp(mu_hat_c + 0.5 * var_hat_c)
E_lambda_a <- exp(mu_hat_a + 0.5 * var_hat_a)

E_lambda; E_lambda_c; E_lambda_a
```

We can represent the distribution of these estimates in the original scale, simulating many random draws to a log-normal distribution centered in the log mean and with the squared root of the variance as log standard deviation. The confidence intervals can be estimated with the function `qlnorm` at 2.5th and 97.5th percentile as:

$$
Y \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu, \sigma^2); \\
Q(p) = \exp(\mu + \sigma \times z_p); z_p = \underline{+}1.96; \\
Q(0.025) = \exp(\mu - 1.96\sigma); \\
Q(0.975) = \exp(\mu + 1.96\sigma)
$$
being $z_p$ the Normal quantile.

![Histograms](figs/Histograms results.jpeg)
A little off, but around the value! How many individuals off, on average? We can answer this by estimating the absolute bias for the parameter $\hat{\Omega} = \lambda$

$$
\text{Bias}(\hat{\bar{\Omega}}) = \hat{\Omega} - \Omega_{true}
$$

```{r}
bias_c <- lambda_c - lambda[,,1]
bias_a <- lambda_a - lambda[,,1]

mean(bias_c); mean(bias_a)
```

Across times and sites, the counts model underestimated abundance by 0.7 individuals on average, while the acoustic model overestimated abundance by 0.05 individuals on average. 

## Sensitivity analysis

We can simulate the dynamic and vary different components fo the model. For example, the research design or decision of the length of sampling days ($T \in \{3, 9, 15, 21, 27\}$). The population mean stationary abundance (low abundant to more abundant; $\mu \in \{\log(1), \log(3) \log(6), \log(12) \log(24)$) and their dynamics by stochastic noise ($\sigma^2 \in \{ 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10\}$) and reversion to the mean stationarity ($c \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$). In these two latter parameters, increasing $\sigma^2$ (more noise) or increasing $c$ (abundance away of stationary mean due to slower reversion) would increase within- and between-site variance. Although explicit between-site heterogeneity will require modeling $\mu_m, \theta_m, $ and $\sigma^2_m$, overall temporal dynamics ($\sigma^2$ and $c$) provide within- and between-site variation, for now. Finally, we can also vary parameters in the observation processes, such as detection probability for the counts (low detectability would produce low counts and poor information on dynamics; $\tau \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$), and the overdispersion parameter for acoustic detections counts; species with sudden peaks of acoustic activity will have higher overdispersion represented in lower values of $\pi$, while species in which their acoustic detections counts are less variable would have higher values of $\pi$; $\pi \in \{0.01,0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25 \}$).

### Temporal variation in sampling length

We can define a grid of visit intensities $V \in \{3,5,10,15,20,25,30\}$


```{r eval=FALSE}
# -------------------------------
# TEMPORAL SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
# -------------------------------
sensi_t1 <- Sys.time()

inits.c <- list(
  list(lmu=1.1,  ltheta=-1.3, lsigsq=-3.1),
  list(lmu=1.5,  ltheta=-1.1, lsigsq=-2.8),
  list(lmu=1.9,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6)
  )

inits.a <- list(
  list(lmu=1.1,  ltheta=-1.3, lsigsq=-3.1, pi = 0.05),
  list(lmu=1.5,  ltheta=-1.1, lsigsq=-2.8, pi = 0.4),
  list(lmu=1.9,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6, pi = 0.75)
  )

# Values of visits per site to test
V <- seq(3,27,3)

# Number of replicates per V
R <- 50   # increase to 50 later

# Storage
results <- list()

for (v in V) {
  
  out_V <- tibble()
  # -------------------------------
  # 1. Build visit matrix T_m
  # -------------------------------
  set.seed(123)
  visit <- sample(v:(v+1), M, replace = TRUE) 
  
  T_m_sen <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))
  
  for(s in 1:S){
    for(m in 1:M){
      sample_idx <- sort(sample(1:T_max, size = visit[m], replace = FALSE))
      sample_vec <- rep(NA, T_max)
      sample_vec[sample_idx] <- 1
      T_m_sen[,m,s] <- sample_vec
    }
  }
  
  # -------------------------------
  # 2. Simulate observations
  # -------------------------------
  set.seed(1234)
  lambda_s <- lambda[, , sp1]   # latent intensity for species 1

  # Counts
  Yc_s_sen <- matrix(NA, T_max, M)
  for (m in 1:M) {
    for (t in 1:T_max) {
      if (!is.na(T_m_sen[t,m,1])) {
        N_bin <- max(1, round(lambda_s[t,m]))
        Yc_s_sen[t,m] <- rbinom(1, N_bin, tau_s[sp1])
      }
    }
  }
  
  # Acoustics
  Ya_s_sen <- matrix(NA, T_max, M)
  for (m in 1:M) {
    for (t in 1:T_max) {
      if (!is.na(T_m_sen[t,m,1])) {
        Ya_s_sen[t,m] <- rnbinom(1, mu = lambda_s[t,m], size = pi_s[sp1])
      }
    }
  }

  # Mask non-visited days
  Yc_s_sen[is.na(T_m_sen[,,1])] <- NA
  Ya_s_sen[is.na(T_m_sen[,,1])] <- NA
    
  # -------------------------------
  # 3. Fit COUNT model
  # -------------------------------
  datalist.dc <- list(
    K = 1,
    M = M,
    qp1 = T_max,
    Y_counts = dcdim(array(Yc_s_sen, dim = c(T_max, M, 1)))
  )

    cat("\n--- Running visits per site =", v, " to",v+1 ,"---\n")

    fit_c <- dc.fit(
      data      = datalist.dc,
      params    = c("c", "a", "sigsq"),
      inits     = inits.c,
      model     = CountOU.dc,
      n.clones  = c(1,2,4,8),
      multiply  = "K",
      unchanged = c("M","qp1"),
      n.chains  = 3,
      n.adapt   = 2000,
      n.update  = 5000,
      thin      = 10,
      n.iter    = 15000
    )

    est_c <- coef(fit_c)
    mu_hat_c <- est_c["a"] / (1 - est_c["c"])

    # -------------------------------
    # 4. Fit ACOUSTIC model
    # -------------------------------
    datalist.dc.a <- list(
      K = 1,
      M = M,
      qp1 = T_max,
      Y_acoust = dcdim(array(Ya_s_sen, dim = c(T_max, M, 1)))
    )
    
    cat("\n--- Running visits per site =", v, " to",v+1 ,"---\n")
    
    fit_a <- dc.fit(
      data      = datalist.dc.a,
      params    = c("c", "a", "sigsq", "pi", "alpha"),
      inits     = inits.a,
      model     = AcoustOU.dc,
      n.clones  = c(1,2,4,8),
      multiply  = "K",
      unchanged = c("M","qp1"),
      n.chains  = 3,
      n.adapt   = 2000,
      n.update  = 5000,
      thin      = 10,
      n.iter    = 15000
    )

    est_a <- coef(fit_a)
    mu_hat_a <- est_a["a"] / (1 - est_a["c"])

    # -------------------------------
    # 5. Store results
    # -------------------------------
    out_V <- bind_rows(out_V,
      tibble(
        v = v,

        # True parameters 
        true_mu = mu_s[sp1],
        true_c = c_s[sp1],
        true_sigsq = sigsq_s[sp1],
        true_pi = pi_s[sp1],
        true_lambda = exp(mu_s[sp1]),

        # Count model estimates
        est_mu_c = mu_hat_c,
        est_c_c = est_c["c"],
        est_sigsq_c = est_c["sigsq"],
        est_lambda_c = exp(mu_hat_c),

        # Acoustic model estimates
        est_mu_a = mu_hat_a,
        est_c_a = est_a["c"],
        est_sigsq_a = est_a["sigsq"],
        est_pi_a = est_a["pi"],
        est_alpha_a = est_a["alpha"],
        est_lambda_a = exp(mu_hat_a)
      )
    )
    cat("\n--- Running visits per site =", v, " to",v+1 ,"---\n")
    
      results[[paste0("V", v)]] <- out_V
}

# Combine all results
res_temporal <- bind_rows(results)
```

### Observation parameters (not yet)

Detection probability for the counts (low detectability would produce low counts and poor information on dynamics; $\tau \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$), and the overdispersion parameter for acoustic detections counts; species with sudden peaks of acoustic activity will have higher overdispersion represented in lower values of $\pi$, while species in which their acoustic detections counts are less variable would have higher values of $\pi$; $\pi \in \{0.01,0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25 \}$).

How we arrive to these ranges?

## Empirical test

### Loading and organizing data

Let's load the file used in `01_data-comparability.Rmd` script. 


This dataset compile four parks with 24 to 31 sites per park ($m$), 51 to 63 species ($s$) sampled in two years (2022-2023). Each site was visited 1 to 5 days. Let's work for now on a species with higher amount of data, during a single year.

First, let extract the acoustic detection rate per minute for two example species


These values could inform a prior $\text{LogNormal}(\mu_{\alpha}, \sigma_{\alpha})$ distribution

$$
\sigma_{\alpha} = \sqrt{\log \left( 1 +\frac{s^2}{m^2} \right)} \\
\mu_{\alpha} = \log(m)-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}
$$
where $s$ is the standard deviation and $m$ is the mean.

So, for example Ovenbird in Acadia
$$
\sigma_{\alpha} = \sqrt{\log \left( 1 +\frac{1.16^2}{2.31^2} \right)} \approx 0.46 \\
\mu_{\alpha} = \log(2.31)-\frac{0.46^2}{2} \approx 0.73 \\
\alpha_{\text{OVEN-ARC}} \sim \text{LogNormal} (0.73, 0.46)
$$

```{r}
alpha_df <- acous_count |>
  filter(year == 2022,
         data_type == "acoustic_data") |>
  mutate(minute = floor_date(as.POSIXct(begin_clock_time, 
                                        format = "%H:%M:%S"), 
                             "minute")) %>%
  group_by(site_id, site_name, year, visit_number, common_name, minute) %>%
  summarise(detections_per_minute = n(), .groups = 'drop') |> 
  group_by(site_name, common_name) |>
  summarise(mean_det_per_min = mean(detections_per_minute),
            sd_det_per_min = sd(detections_per_minute, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = 'drop') |> 
  filter(common_name %in% c("Red-eyed Vireo", 
                            "Ovenbird")) |>
  mutate(sigma_alpha = sqrt(log(1 + (sd_det_per_min^2 / mean_det_per_min^2))),
         mu_alpha    = log(mean_det_per_min) - (sigma_alpha^2 / 2)) |>
  arrange(common_name)
```

How to reconcile time of detection of each record from acoustic detection or point counts? 

While the `point_count` data include the `observation_time` variable, this information for the `acoustic_data` is at the `begin_clock_time` variable. Let's adjust this with the function `coalesce` from `dplyr` in `tidyverse`. Then, we can consolidate the "initial temporal window" per visit in each site_id with the detection time.

```{r}
acoust_count_summary <- acous_count_filt |> 
  # dummy column to unify time of detection either by count or 
  mutate(detection_time = coalesce(observation_time, begin_clock_time)) |>
  # initial temporal window
  group_by(site_id, date) |>
  mutate(time_window = min(hms::as_hms(detection_time), na.rm = TRUE),
         time_window = hms::as_hms(time_window),
         DateTime = as.POSIXct(paste(date, time_window), format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
         Time_window = floor_date(DateTime, "10 min")) |>
  # First summarization to extract sum of counts per point count and number of acoustic detections
  group_by(site_name, site_id, date, common_name, data_type, Time_window) |>
  summarise(abundance = sum(abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
         acous_detections = n()) |>
  # Second summarization to extract maximum number of counts or mean acoustic detections counts per day
  group_by(site_name, site_id, date, common_name, Time_window) |>
  summarise(counts = max(abundance, na.rm = TRUE),
         acous_detections = max(acous_detections)) |>
  as.data.frame() |> 
  arrange(Time_window)

str(acoust_count_summary)
```

And now we can prepare these data for data cloning

```{r}
SPP_a_df <- SPP_grid |>

              select(date, site_id, acous_detections),
            by = c("date", "site_id")) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = site_id,
              values_from = acous_detections) |>
  arrange(date)
```

### Fit model to empirical data - point counts

Recall the model:
```{r Stochastic GSS model for data cloning fitting of point counts}
CountOU.dc <- function() {

  # Priors (no cloning)
  lmu ~ dnorm(log(3.14), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  ltheta ~ dnorm(log(0.3), 1/(0.2^2)) # in precision terms
  lsigsq ~ dnorm(log(0.05), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
#  ltau ~ dnorm(log(0.3/(1-0.3)), 1/(0.5^2)) # logit-normal 
  
#  tau <- 1/(1+exp(-ltau))  # detection probability
  tau <- 0.3 #fixing tau close to true value to evaluate convergence and informability
  mu <- lmu
  theta <- exp(ltheta)
  sigsq <- exp(lsigsq)
  
  c <- exp(-theta)
  a <- mu * (1-c)
  Vinf <- sigsq/(1-exp(-2 * theta))
  
  # Likelihood (data cloning)
  for (k in 1:K) {               # K = clones
    for (m in 1:M) {             # M = sites
      
      # Stationary distribution for t=1
      X1[1,m,k] ~ dnorm(mu, 1 / Vinf) # JAGS works with precision

      # State process over time
      for (t in 2:qp1) {
        X1[t,m,k] ~ dnorm((a + c * X1[t-1,m,k]), 1 / sigsq) # JAGS works with precision
      }

      # Observation processes
      for (t in 1:qp1) {
        # point count Poisson detection
        Y_counts[t,m,k] ~ dpois(exp(X1[t,m,k]) * tau)
      }
    }
  }
}

```

Bundle empirical data and fit the model with data cloning.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
  list(lmu=1.9,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6)
  )

SPPdatalist.dc.c <- list(
```

### Fit model to empirical data - acoustic detections counts

```{r}
alpha_df
```


Recall the model:

```{r Stochastic GSS model for data cloning fitting of point counts}
AcoustOU2.dc <- function() {

  # Priors (no cloning)
  lmu ~ dnorm(log(3), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  ltheta ~ dnorm(log(0.3), 1/(0.2^2)) # in precision terms
  lsigsq ~ dnorm(log(0.05), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  pi ~ dnorm(0.17, 1/(0.01^2)) 
  alpha ~ dlnorm(0.243, 1/(0.671^2)) # scaling between abundance and acoustic counts - change per species-site
  
  mu <- lmu
  theta <- exp(ltheta)
  sigsq <- exp(lsigsq)
  
  c <- exp(-theta)
  a <- mu * (1-c)
  Vinf <- sigsq/(1-exp(-2 * theta))
  
   # Likelihood (data cloning)
  for (k in 1:K) {               # K = clones
    for (m in 1:M) {             # M = sites
      
      # Stationary distribution for t=1
      X1[1,m,k] ~ dnorm(mu, 1 / Vinf) # JAGS works with precision

      # State process over time
      for (t in 2:qp1) {
        X1[t,m,k] ~ dnorm((a + c * X1[t-1,m,k]), 1 / sigsq) # JAGS works with precision
      }

      # Observation processes
      for (t in 1:qp1) {
        # Acoustic Negative Binomial detection
        # we should re-parameterize lambda and pi to p
        # p = pi/(pi+lambda)
        lambda_ac[t,m,k] <- exp(X1[t,m,k]) * alpha
        p_nb[t,m,k] <- pi / (pi + lambda_ac[t,m,k])
        Y_acoust[t,m,k] ~ dnegbin(p_nb[t,m,k], pi)
      }
    }
  }
}

```

And we can bundle the data and fit the model with data cloning.
```{r, eval=FALSE}

  list(lmu=1.9,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6, pi = 0.1)
  )

SPPdatalist.dc.a <- list( 
  K = 1, # clones start at 1 
  M = length(unique(acoust_count_summary$site_id)), # number of sites

  )

start_time <- Sys.time()
dcrun.GSS.a.SPP <- dc.fit(data = SPPdatalist.dc.a,
                    params = c("c", "a", "sigsq", "pi", "alpha"),

duration_model <- Sys.time()-start_time
print(duration_model)
```

With the MLEs, we can reconstruct the OU trajectories:

$$
\hat{X}_{m,t} \sim \text{Normal}\left(\frac{\hat{a}}{1-\hat{c}}, \frac{\hat{\sigma^2}}{1-\hat{c}^2}\right); \\

\hat{\lambda}_{t,m} = \exp(\hat{X}_{t,m})
$$

and then compare the latent expected abundance
$$
\lambda_{t,m}^{(\text{counts})} ~ \text{vs} ~ \lambda_{t,m}^{(\text{acoust})}
$$

```{r}

spp_sites_times <- data.frame(species = c(rep("OVEN", 4), 
                                          rep("REVI", 4)),
                              site_name = rep(c("ARC", "HBE", "KWW", "MBR"),2),
                              M_s = c(15,18,14,24,
                                      12,17,12,24),
                              T_max = c(28,74,31,29,
                                       57,74,34,29))

model_types <- c("c", "a")
lambda_h <- list()

for (i in 1:nrow(spp_sites_times)) {
  species_i <- spp_sites_times$species[i]
  site_i    <- spp_sites_times$site_name[i]
  m_s       <- spp_sites_times$M_s[i]
  t_s       <- spp_sites_times$T_max[i]

  for (type in model_types) {

    # Build model name
    model_name <- paste0(species_i, "_", type, "_", site_i)

    # Retrieve model object
    model_obj <- get(model_name)

    # Extract coefficients depending on model type
    coefs <- coef(model_obj)

    if (type == "c") {
      a_hat     <- coefs[1]
      c_hat     <- coefs[2]
      sigsq_hat <- coefs[3]
    } else if (type == "a") {
      a_hat     <- coefs[1]
      c_hat     <- coefs[3]
      sigsq_hat <- coefs[5]
    }

    # Derived quantities
    mu_hat  <- a_hat / (1 - c_hat)
    var_hat <- sigsq_hat / (1 - c_hat^2)

    # Simulate X_hat
    X_hat <- matrix(NA, nrow = t_s, ncol = m_s)
    X_hat[1, ] <- rnorm(m_s, mu_hat, sqrt(var_hat))

    for (t in 2:t_s) {
      X_hat[t, ] <- rnorm(m_s, a_hat + c_hat * X_hat[t - 1, ], sqrt(sigsq_hat))
    }

    lambda_hat <- exp(X_hat)

    # Store results with unique name
    lambda_h[[model_name]] <- lambda_hat
  }
}

```

```{r}
lambda_df <- imap_dfr(lambda_h, function(mat, nm) {
  
  # split name into components
  parts <- strsplit(nm, "_")[[1]]
  species <- parts[1]
  model   <- parts[2]   # c = point counts, a = acoustic
  area    <- parts[3]
  
  tibble(
    lambda = as.vector(mat),
    species = species,
    model = ifelse(model == "c", "Count", "Acoustic"),
    area = area
  )
})

lambda_df_summary <- lambda_df %>%
  group_by(species, area, model) %>%
  summarise(
    mean = mean(lambda, na.rm = TRUE),
    lwr  = quantile(lambda, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
    upr  = quantile(lambda, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(lambda_df, aes(x = lambda, fill = model, color = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_rug(alpha = 0.2, sides = "b") +
   # 95% CI lines
  geom_vline(data = lambda_df_summary,
             aes(xintercept = lwr, color = model),
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(data = lambda_df_summary,
             aes(xintercept = upr, color = model),
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Mean line
  geom_vline(data = lambda_df_summary,
             aes(xintercept = mean, color = model),
             linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_grid(species ~ area, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,15))+

  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    x = "Expected abundance (λ)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Model type",
    color = "Model type"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Time series

```{r}
mat_to_ts <- function(mat, nm) {
  parts <- strsplit(nm, "_")[[1]]
  species <- parts[1]
  model   <- ifelse(parts[2] == "c", "Count", "Acoustic")
  area    <- parts[3]
  
  as_tibble(mat) %>%
    mutate(time = row_number()) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -time,
      names_to = "site",
      values_to = "lambda"
    ) %>%
    mutate(species = species,
           model = model,
           area = area)
}

lambda_h_ts_df <- imap_dfr(lambda_h, mat_to_ts)

lambda_ts_mean <- lambda_h_ts_df %>%
  group_by(species, area, model, time) %>%
  summarise(mean_lambda = mean(lambda), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(lambda_h_ts_df, aes(x = time, y = lambda, color = model)) +
   facet_grid(species ~ area, scales = "free_x") +
  geom_point(aes(group = factor(area)), alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_line(data = lambda_ts_mean,
            aes(x = time, y = mean_lambda, color = model),
            linewidth = 1.4) +
   scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,15))+
  labs(
    x = "Time",
    y = "Expected abundance (λ)",
    color = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_classic()+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```



```{r}
a_hat_a_SPP <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a.SPP)[1]
c_hat_a_SPP <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a.SPP)[2]
sig_hat_a_SPP <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a.SPP)[4]

mu_hat_a_SPP <- a_hat_a_SPP / (1 - c_hat_a_SPP)
var_hat_a_SPP <- sig_hat_a_SPP / (1 - c_hat_a_SPP^2)

X_hat_a_SPP <- matrix(NA, nrow = T_max_SPP, ncol = M_SPP)

# Initialize from stationary distribution
X_hat_a_SPP[1,] <- rnorm(M_SPP, mu_hat_a_SPP, sqrt(var_hat_a_SPP))

# OU/Gompertz dynamics
for (t in 2:T_max_SPP){
  X_hat_a_SPP[t,] <- rnorm(M_SPP, (a_hat_a_SPP + c_hat_a_SPP * X_hat_a_SPP[t-1,]), sqrt(sig_hat_a_SPP))
}

lambda_a_SPP <- exp(X_hat_a_SPP)
```


Given the Janzen inequality, we can contrast also the stationary expectations

$$
\text{E}(\lambda) = \text{E}[\exp(X)] = \exp\left(\mu + 0.5 \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2}\right)
$$

```{r}

E_lambda_c_SPP <- exp(mu_hat_c_SPP + 0.5 * var_hat_c_SPP)
E_lambda_a_SPP <- (exp(mu_hat_a_SPP + 0.5 * var_hat_a_SPP))
```

It seems we need a scaling parameter! In this case, the mean acoustic detections counts are 20.34, while the expected mean abundance from point counts is 7.16. This is a radii of 0.35; $\text{E}(\lambda) \approx $
